Humans have always wanted to know where we came from. So we invented stories that served as believable explanations. From the Abrahamic religions, to Greek, Roman, Norse and Egyptian mythology, to the Australian Aboriginal dreamtime stories, to Hinduism and so on. All of these were somewhat isolated attempts to explain where we came from and where we're going. The answer was usually: we were created by magical, omnipotent beings, and if we are nice to people and believe in those magical, omnipotent beings, then life after death that will be better than this life. These were all very nice explanations. With little evidence to the contrary, the removal of the uncertainty of not knowing where we came from and where we were going, and the threats from the various churches and holy books, it was very hard not to be religious.

Then, actual explanations for the formation of human life on Earth began to emerge. Ones that were backed by observation and deduction. Darwin came up with very convincing evidence that humans were not created by a divine being, but instead evolved over hundreds of millions of years. Eventually, even the Catholic church acknowledged that humans were not created directly by God as clearly stated in the bible. We don't yet have the full picture, but we are constantly finding new puzzle pieces. It's only a matter of time before the puzzle is complete and theistic religions become fully obsolete. Atheism is the natural evolution of religious beliefs. Religion is, slowly but surely, dying. Will it lead to a utopia? No, but it will certainly make things better.

It's been almost four years since 38 Studios shut down, but the fallout from its collapse--and the subsequent defaulting on a massive loan from the taxpayers of Rhode Island--continues. The Securities and Exchange Commission today charged Wells Fargo Securities and the Rhode Island Commerce Corporation (formerly the Rhode Island Economic Development Corporation) with defrauding investors in the issuing of $75 million in bonds to loan the studio money. After setting aside money for bond-offering expenses, a reserve fund and a capitalized interest fund, the RIEDC loaned the remaining $50 million to 38 Studios for the development of its Project Copernicus massively multiplayer online game, with the money to be repaid from the game's revenues. However, the SEC alleges that 38 Studios had told both the RIEDC and Wells Fargo that it would need $75 million to finish the game, but that information wasn't passed on.
